lead: A reading from a sensor is an estimate, not a verdict. The true value is hidden; what we have is a number plus the effects of blunders, bias and noise. Error analysis separates those effects, and statistics turns repeated readings into a mean and a believable uncertainty. This chapter builds the sentence that every calibration certificate and lab report must contain: best estimate ± uncertainty, with the method stated. It is used in watt-hour meter testing, ECG front ends, IRCTC coach temperature loggers and any place where a decision depends on a measured number.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.4 for bias, precision and resolution, and Chapter 1.3 for the calibration deviations that feed the systematic uncertainty.

sections.h3: Three kinds of error, and what averaging does

blocks.text: A measurement error is the difference between the reading and the true value: absolute error = xm − xtrue, where xm is the measured value and xtrue is the accepted true value. Relative error = (xm − xtrue)/xtrue. Percentage error = relative error × 100 %. The correction is the negative of the error; add it to the reading to make the reading better.

items: Gross error or blunder: misread display, wrong range, wrong unit. Statistics does not cure it; repeat the measurement.
Systematic error or bias: calibration offset, scale-factor error, loading, drift. It has the same sign and roughly the same size on every repeat.
Random error: noise, vibration, supply ripple, thermal agitation. It changes sign and size from reading to reading.

blocks.text: The two error types respond differently to averaging. A bias of +0.2 V keeps the mean +0.2 V high no matter how many readings you take. Random scatter with standard deviation s falls to s/√n in the mean of n independent readings. That is why a calibration offset must be found from a standard, not from many repeats.

sections.h3: Mean, spread and the uncertainty of the mean

blocks.text: Take n repeated readings x<sub>1</sub>, x<sub>2</sub>, …, x<sub>n</sub> at the same input. The best estimate of the true value is the sample mean x̄ = Σx<sub>i</sub>/n. The median is the middle value when the readings are sorted. The range is the largest reading minus the smallest. Median and range are quick checks; the mean and standard deviation use all the data.

blocks.where: s² is the sample variance, in squared units of the reading; x<sub>i</sub> is one reading; x̄ is the sample mean; n is the number of readings. Use n − 1 because the deviations are measured from x̄, not from the unknown true value. Dividing by n understates the scatter.

s is the sample standard deviation, in the reading's units; s<sub>x̄</sub> is the standard uncertainty of the mean, also called the standard error; k = 1, 2, 3 gives roughly 68 %, 95 %, 99 % confidence if the scatter is normal.

blocks.text: Draw a histogram of the deviations. The normal distribution is a fair model when many small independent random effects act, the histogram is roughly symmetric, and there is no drift or outlier. It is a poor model for a warm-up drift or a single loose connection.

sections.h3: Combining uncertainties, resolution and a straight-line fit

blocks.where: u<sub>a</sub> and u<sub>b</sub> are standard uncertainties of a and b, in their units; u<sub>y</sub> is the standard uncertainty of the result y, in the same units as y.

blocks.text: y = ab or y = a/b  →  u<sub>y</sub>/|y| = √((u<sub>a</sub>/a)² + (u<sub>b</sub>/b)²)
blocks.where: u<sub>y</sub>/|y| is the fractional uncertainty of y; u<sub>a</sub>/a and u<sub>b</sub>/b are fractional uncertainties of the inputs. For a power law y = a<sup>n</sup> (a raised to the power n) with exact n, multiply the fractional uncertainty of a by |n|: u<sub>y</sub>/|y| = |n| × u<sub>a</sub>/|a|.

blocks.text: The display resolution adds a rectangular uncertainty of ± half the last digit. For a 0.01 V display, half the last digit is 0.005 V. Convert it to a standard uncertainty by dividing by √3, giving 0.0029 V, then combine it in quadrature with the scatter. A straight-line fit y = mx + c gives slope m = [nΣxy − ΣxΣy]/[nΣx² − (Σx)²] and intercept c = (Σy − mΣx)/n. The correlation coefficient r near +1 or −1 says the line is a good model; r near 0 says it is not. Reject an outlier only with a stated rule, such as more than 3s from the mean plus a recorded physical cause.

examples.question: Ten readings of a 5.000 V reference are 5.01, 4.98, 5.02, 4.99, 5.00, 5.03, 4.97, 5.01, 4.99 and 5.00 V. The display resolves 0.01 V. Find the mean, the bias, the sample standard deviation, the standard uncertainty of the mean, and the 95 % confidence interval. Compare the resolution contribution with the scatter.
steps: Resolution: half the last digit = 0.01/2 = 0.005 V = 5 mV. Standard uncertainty = 5/√3 = 2.887 mV. Combine it with the scatter in quadrature: u = √(5.774² + 2.887²) = √(33.34 + 8.33) = √41.67 = 6.455 mV. The scatter term is about twice the resolution term, so scatter dominates but does not erase it.

At 95 %, k = 2, so the half-width is 2 × 6.455 = 12.91 mV ≈ 12.9 mV. Interval: 5.000 V ± 12.9 mV, about 4.987 V to 5.013 V. With only n = 10 readings, k = 2 is an approximation valid for large n; the exact factor from the t-distribution is t₉ = 2.26, which widens the interval slightly.
examples.answer: Mean = 5.000 V, bias = 0.000 V, s = 18.257 mV, standard uncertainty of the mean = 5.774 mV, resolution standard uncertainty = 2.887 mV, combined standard uncertainty u = √(5.774² + 2.887²) = 6.455 mV, 95 % interval = 5.000 V ± 12.9 mV (about 4.987 V to 5.013 V). Scatter is about twice the resolution term, so scatter dominates but does not erase it.
examples.check:
import math
x = [5.01, 4.98, 5.02, 4.99, 5.00, 5.03, 4.97, 5.01, 4.99, 5.00]
n = len(x)
s = sum(x)
m = s / n
b = m - 5.000
d = [(v - m) * 1000 for v in x]
ss = sum(t * t for t in d)
s2 = ss / (n - 1)
sd = math.sqrt(s2)
sem = sd / math.sqrt(n)
res = 0.01 * 1000 / 2 / math.sqrt(3)
u = math.hypot(sem, res)
ci = 2 * u
for v in (s, m, b, ss, s2, sd, sem, res, u, ci):
    print(f"{v:.3f}")

traps: Dividing by n instead of n − 1 in the sample variance understates s and makes the result look better than it is.
Adding uncertainties arithmetically instead of in quadrature. For independent random errors, squares add.
Quoting s of one reading when the question asks for the uncertainty of the mean. The mean's uncertainty is s/√n.
Treating half the last digit as a standard uncertainty. It is a rectangular half-width; divide by √3 before combining.
Stopping at the scatter and forgetting the resolution term. Combine both in quadrature before quoting the interval.
Deleting an outlier just because it looks bad. State a rejection rule and record the physical cause.

quiz.q: Define absolute error, relative error and correction. State the sign convention used here.
quiz.a: Absolute error = x_m − x_true. Relative error = (x_m − x_true)/x_true. Correction = −(absolute error). A positive error means the reading is high.

quiz.q: Why does averaging ten readings not remove a calibration offset?
quiz.a: A calibration offset is systematic: it has the same sign and size on every reading. The mean is shifted by the same offset. Averaging shrinks only the random part, from s to s/√n.

quiz.q: Four readings are 10.02, 10.00, 9.98 and 10.01 V. Find the mean, the sample standard deviation and the standard uncertainty of the mean.
For y = ab, a = 20.0 ± 1.0 and b = 5.0 ± 0.1. Find y and its standard uncertainty.
quiz.a: y = 20.0 × 5.0 = 100.0 in the unit of a × the unit of b (for example, if a is in volts and b in amperes, y is 100.0 W). Fractional uncertainties: 1.0/20.0 = 0.05 and 0.1/5.0 = 0.02; these are dimensionless. Combined fractional uncertainty = √(0.05² + 0.02²) = 0.05385. u_y = 100.0 × 0.05385 = 5.385 ≈ 5.4, in the same unit as y.

quiz.q: A display resolves 0.01 V. The scatter of one reading is s = 0.002 V and n = 16. Which contribution dominates the uncertainty of the mean? Show numbers.
quiz.a: Resolution standard uncertainty = (0.01/2)/√3 = 0.002887 V = 2.887 mV. Standard uncertainty of the mean from scatter = s/√n = 0.002/√16 = 0.002/4 = 0.0005 V = 0.5 mV. Resolution dominates because 2.887 mV is much larger than 0.5 mV.

quiz.q: A reading lies 4s from the mean. What is the correct way to handle it?
quiz.a: Do not delete it silently. Check for a cause such as a loose connection or wrong range. If a rejection rule was stated in advance, apply it and report that the point was removed. Otherwise keep it and report the result with and without it.

quiz.q: What does k = 2 mean in x̄ ± k·s/√n?
quiz.a: If the scatter is normal, the interval x̄ ± 2s/√n covers roughly 95 % of the distribution of the mean. The factor 2 is valid for large n; for small n the t-distribution factor is larger.

quiz.q: When is the normal distribution a fair model for a histogram of repeated readings?
quiz.a: When many small independent random effects act, the histogram is roughly symmetric, and there is no drift or outlier. A skewed histogram or a warm-up trend calls for a different model.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry writes uncertainty statements using the GUM framework, separating Type A uncertainty from repeated readings and Type B uncertainty from certificates and specifications. Calibration laboratories often check these intervals with Monte Carlo simulation. Sensor drift over months is studied with Allan variance, which separates white noise from bias instability. Search for GUM measurement uncertainty, Type A and Type B uncertainty, least-squares calibration and Allan variance.
